name: Life of Fred
line: Life of Fred teaches math in chapters of a story, in one order. In AMP, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Life of Fred: Life of Fred teaches math in chapters of a story, in one order. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
verdict: Life of Fred teaches math as a story about Fred, in chapters meant to be read in order, each followed by questions whose answers are printed on the next page [3][4]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Life of Fred the unit is the chapter: part of a story about Fred, then a short set of questions [3][4]. Cathy Duffy writes that the text concentrates on concepts more than on computation practice and drill [4]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [10].

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after, right or wrong, updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem. Life of Fred's books are meant to be used in order, and every learner meets the same chapters in the same sequence [3][4]. The learner checks their own answers against the page that follows [4].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After each problem AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. In Life of Fred the answers are printed on the next page, and the learner checks them [4]. The site that sells the series says the books do not give step-by-step answers to every question [2]. Across 40 studies of computer feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect [8].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a learner shows a skill by getting it right without help, more than once, and moves on. An answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In Life of Fred the next step is the next chapter, and the adult or the learner sets the pace [3][4].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. In Life of Fred, ideas carry forward: functions met in one book return in a later one [4]. We found no schedule for reviewing earlier topics in the reviews we read [3][4]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [9].

rows.range: Grade 1 through algebra, geometry and trigonometry, then calculus, statistics and linear algebra [3][4][5].
rows.start: The adult chooses a book to begin with. The books are meant to be used in order [3][4].
rows.teaching: Chapters of a story about Fred, a five-year-old math teacher, each followed by short question sets. Applications often come before the method [3][4].
rows.next: The next chapter, in the same order for every learner. The adult or the learner sets the pace [3][4].
rows.mastery: None found in the pages we read [3]. The learner checks answers printed on the next page [4].
rows.review: None found in the pages we read [3][4]. Some ideas return in later books [4].
rows.print: The whole course is printed books, the same for every learner, with the answers inside [3][4].
rows.adult: Chooses the book, checks answers with the keys in the books, and sets the pace. How much the adult teaches varies [3][4].
rows.reports: None found in the pages we read [3][4].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found on its sites, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [1][2][6][7].

theirs: Life of Fred is a series of math books written by Dr. Stanley Schmidt [3] and published by Polka Dot Publishing [1]. Cathy Duffy, a reviewer of homeschool curricula, describes him as a retired math teacher [3][4]. The series runs from elementary books for grade 1 through fractions, decimals and percents, pre-algebra, algebra, geometry and trigonometry, and on to calculus, statistics and linear algebra [3][4][5].

Each chapter is part of a story about Fred, a five-year-old math teacher, and applications often come before the method [3][4]. The learner reads, then answers a short set of "Your Turn to Play" questions, with the answers on the next page [4]. Chapters end with problem sets, and separate Zillions of Practice Problems books add practice [3][5]. The books are written for independent study and meant to be used in order [3][4].
credit: Math told as a story, with humor that wins over learners who dislike worksheets [3][4].
Applications come before the method, and proofs begin early [3].
Written for a learner to work through alone, with the answers in the book [3][4].

theirs: We found no outcome study of Life of Fred on its sites [1][2], in Evidence for ESSA [6] or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [7].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect (0.49), giving the correct answer 0.32, and marking right or wrong only 0.05; the studies mix ages and subjects [8]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [9]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: Your child loves a story and learns best by reading.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no tests to give.
You want every answer checked at once and followed by the worked steps.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
Your child reads Fred and you want daily practice beside the books.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Life of Fred?
questions.answer: Life of Fred teaches in chapters of a story, in a fixed order, and the learner checks answers printed in the book [3][4]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Life of Fred work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of Life of Fred on its sites, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [1][2][6][7].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. A learner can read Fred for the story and the ideas and practice in AMP, which places them from their first answers.
